title: 5 Best ChatGPT Prompts for API Design (2026)
description: Design a REST or RPC API the disciplined way — resources, contracts, errors, versioning, and a review against real-world usage — in five prompts.

steps.title: Model the resources
steps.promptText:
You are an API architect. I'm building: [ONE-PARAGRAPH PRODUCT DESCRIPTION]. Consumers: [WHO CALLS IT — web app / mobile / third parties].

Propose the resource model: entities, their relationships, and which ones deserve top-level endpoints vs. nesting. Present as a table: resource | key fields | relationships | endpoint style. Flag anything in my description that suggests a resource I haven't named.
steps.whyThisTool: ChatGPT rapidly maps fuzzy product descriptions onto clean resource models.
steps.outputExpected: A resource table plus at least one 'you also need X' catch.

steps.title: Draft the endpoint contract
steps.promptText: For the [RESOURCE] resource, draft the full contract: endpoints (method + path), request/response JSON shapes with realistic example values, pagination style, filtering params, and idempotency behavior for each write. Use [REST/GraphQL/RPC] conventions consistently.
steps.whyThisTool: Concrete example payloads expose design problems that abstract schemas hide.
steps.outputExpected: A contract you could hand to a frontend dev today, with realistic examples.

steps.title: Design the error model
steps.promptText: Design the error model for this API: error response shape, a table of error codes (HTTP status | machine code | when it happens | what the client should do), and how validation errors report multiple field failures at once. Make retryable vs. non-retryable explicit.
steps.whyThisTool: Error models are always an afterthought — making them a dedicated step fixes that.
steps.outputExpected: An error table where every row tells the client what to DO, not just what went wrong.

steps.title: Stress-test with real sequences
steps.promptText: Simulate three real client sessions against this contract: (1) the happy-path first-time flow, (2) a flaky-network client that retries everything, (3) a third-party integrator doing bulk sync. Write out each request sequence, and flag every point where the API is awkward, chatty, or ambiguous.
steps.whyThisTool: Walking concrete call sequences finds the N+1s and ambiguities reviews miss.
steps.outputExpected: Three annotated request sequences with specific awkwardness flags.

steps.title: Versioning and evolution plan
steps.promptText: Recommend a versioning strategy for this API (URL / header / field deprecation) given [EXPECTED CONSUMERS]. Then list which parts of the current design are most likely to change and how the contract lets them evolve WITHOUT a breaking version bump. End with a checklist I can run before any future change ships.
steps.whyThisTool: Evolution planning at design time is 10x cheaper than a v2 migration later.
steps.outputExpected: A one-page strategy plus a pre-ship breaking-change checklist.

faq.a: Yes — say GraphQL in step 2 and the contract step produces types/queries/mutations instead of endpoints. Steps 1, 3, 4 and 5 are paradigm-independent.

faq.q: Can I skip straight to step 2?
faq.a: If your resource model is already settled, yes. But step 1's 'resource you haven't named' catch pays for itself surprisingly often.

faq.q: Which AI is best for API design?
faq.a: ChatGPT and Claude are both strong. We verify against GPT-5.1; Claude tends to write longer rationales, which some teams prefer for design docs.

benefit: Ship an API contract that survives real clients — no v2 rewrite in six months.
